section.p: Based on

the written pleadings of the Parties along with Annexes, in particular the statement of claim by the Claimant dated May 08, 2013, the written pleading of the Claimant dated September 24, 2013, the written pleading of the Respondent dated September 30, 2013, the written pleading of the Respondent dated October 16, 2013, the written pleading of the Claimant dated October 17, 2013, the response by the Respondent dated January 01, 2014 (in English dated December 06, 2013), the reply of the Claimant dated January 29, 2014, the rejoinder of the Respondent dated February 26, 2014, the written pleading of the Claimant dated April 28, 2014, the written pleading of the Claimant dated April 30, 2014, the written pleading of the Respondent dated May 08, 2014, the written pleading of the Claimant dated May 22, 2014, the written pleading of the Respondent dated May 27, 2014, the written pleading of the Claimant dated July 17, 2014, the written pleading of the Respondent dated July 17, 2014, the written pleading of the Claimant dated September 25, 2014, the written pleading of the Respondent dated September 25, 2014, the written pleading of the Claimant dated February 10, 2015, the written pleading of the Respondent dated February 10, 2015, the written pleading of the Respondent dated March 03, 2015, the written pleading of the Claimant dated March 30, 2015, the written pleading of the Respondent dated April 01, 2015, the written pleadings of the Claimant and Respondent each dated June 08, 2015, the written pleading of the Claimant dated June 18, 2015, the written pleading of the Respondent dated June 22, 2015, the written pleading of the Claimant dated July 20, 2015, and the written pleading of the Respondent dated July 21, 2015 (hereinafter jointly referred to as the “Written Pleadings”),
the arbitral tribunal hereby issues the following

p.bd: to transfer the trademarks “STABILIGRID,” reg. no. 4,259,085 and “HOOFGRID,” reg. no. 4,269,608, entered in the Register of the United States Patent and Trademark Office, to the Claimant and for this purpose to give its consent to the United States Patent and Trademark Office to transfer the trademarks to the Claimant and to submit the required declarations, and

to transfer the trademarks “STABILIGRID,” application no. 1559381, and “HOOFGRID,” application no. 1559376, registered with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office, to the Claimant and to give its consent to the Canadian Intellectual Property Office to record the transfer of rights in the registration files and to submit all of the declarations required for such purpose.

The Respondent is ordered to refrain from using the trademarks “STABILIGRID” and/or “HOOFGRID” without the Claimant’s consent in business dealings in North America in connection with soil stabilization systems, particularly with the soil stabilization system “ECOGRID,“ in particular from affixing the aforementioned trademarks to the above designated products or their presentation or packaging, from offering the above designated products under the above designated marks, from placing them on the market or possessing, importing, or exporting them for the aforementioned purposes and lastly from using the aforementioned marks in business documentation or in advertising.

The Respondent is ordered to provide information to the Claimant on the origin and the distribution channels of the goods described above in subparagraph II, in particular to provide information regarding
names and addresses of the manufacturers, suppliers, and the commercial customers and sales outlets for which they were intended and
the quantity of the goods produced, delivered, received, or ordered as well as the prices paid for the goods at issue.
The Respondent is ordered to pay to the Claimant a minimum flat-rate compensation for damages of EUR 20,000.00.

It is determined that the Respondent is obligated to reimburse the Claimant for all damage, which has arisen or will arise in the future to the Claimant in connection with the failure to apply for and register the trademarks “STABILIGRID,” “HOOFGRID,” and “HOMEGRID” in the U.S.A. and in Canada as per section H (7) of the distributor agreement of April 09, 2008, the transfer of the trademarks in accordance with subparagraph I of the unlawful use of the “STABILIGRID” and/or “HOOFGRID” trademarks and in particular the actions designated under subparagraph II while the minimum flat-rate compensation for damages as per subparagraph IV. is to be credited.

The Respondent is ordered to bear the cost of the legal dispute including the cost incurred in the course of the mediation carried out. The amount of such cost to be borne and a subsequent order to refund cost shall remain reserved to a separate arbitral award on cost.

section.p: The arbitral award is based on the following

item.p: The subject matter of the dispute between the parties is a claim asserted by the Claimant against the Respondent for the transfer of the “HOOFGRID” and “STABILIGRID” trademarks. In addition, the Claimant asserts a claim for injunctive relief against the Respondent with regard to the use of these marks in the course of trade in connection with soil stabilization systems. In addition, the parties are involved in a dispute for claims for compensation for damages on the part of the Claimant from the Respondent. The Claimant requests the payment of a flat rate amount of compensation for damages, as well as the determination that the Respondent should be obligated to pay compensation to the Claimant for damages in connection with the failure to apply for and register the “HOOFGRID,” “STABILIGRID,” and “HOMEGRID” trademarks, the transfer of these trademarks, as well as the claimed unlawful use of these trademarks by the Respondent.

The Claimant is a company with limited liability formed in 1994, entered in the commercial register of Hof Local Court under HBR 2231 with headquarters in Arzberg. The Claimant has used the company name PURUS PLASITICS [sic] GmbH since January 2012 (formerly purus Arzberg GmbH). The company is active in the area of plastics recycling and plastic injection molding production.

The company name of the Respondent is Eco-Terr Distributing, Inc. It was entered in the commercial register of the U.S. state of Washington on April 07, 2006. It sells products for use in the construction industry.

The parties entered into a distributor agreement on April 09, 2008 (“Distributor Agreement,” Exhibit SK2), in which the Claimant transferred to the Respondent the distribution of the soil stabilization system ECOGRID (“Contractual Product”) in North America (Canada and the U.S.A.). This Distributor Agreement entered into force on the same date.

The Claimant – referred to in the Distributor Agreement as “purus” – granted the Respondent – referred to in the Distributor Agreement as the “Sales Partner” – in Section H (6) of the Distributor Agreement the sole right to distribute the contractual product in the contractual territory under the names HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, or HOMEGRID. Section H (6) of the Distributor Agreement states:
“6. The Sales Partner has the sole right to distribute the contractual product under the names HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, or HOMEGRID in the contractual territory. The Sales Partner is not entitled to distribute the product under any trademark other than ECORASTER, ECOGRID, HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, or HOMEGRID. ”

The Respondent also entered into an obligation in Section H (7) of the Distributor Agreement to apply for registration of the names HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOMEGRID as trademarks in the U.S.A. and Canada within 6 months after signing the Distributor Agreement (“6-month period”). Section H (7) of the Distributor Agreement contains the following provision in this respect:
“7. The Sales Partner shall be obligated to apply for the registration of the names HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOMEGRID as trademarks exclusively for the contractual products (the “Trademarks”) with the United States Patent and Trademark Office and with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office within 6 months from the signing of this agreement. The Sales Partner is to do everything necessary in order to achieve the registration of the trademarks for it without undue delay; any and all cost associated with the registration shall be borne by the Sales Partner. The design of the trademarks HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOMEGRID is to be in line with the design of the brands ECORASTER and ECOGRID. The design of the trademarks HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOMEGRID shall require the prior written consent of purus before an application is made for registration of the names as trademarks.”

Section H (8) Distributor Agreement provides that the Respondent is to transfer the trademarks HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOMEGRID to the Claimant with effect as of the date of the ending of the Distributor Agreement and the Claimant will accept such transfer. Section H (8) Distributor Agreement states as follows:
“8. The Sales Partner hereby transfers the trademarks to purus effective from the day of the termination of this agreement. purus hereby accepts such transfer. Any and all other rights and the registrations in the United States of America, in Canada, and abroad with regard to the trademarks, the goodwill associated with the trademarks, as well as any and all rights, which are acquired by their use, shall likewise be transferred. The Sales Partner shall authorize the registration of the transfer of rights in the relevant register. The Sales Partner shall take all steps, which are required or requested by purus in order to facilitate and secure the legally valid acquisition of the trademarks by purus and the registrations of purus as the proprietor of the trademarks. After termination of this agreement, the Sales Partner shall hand over to purus any and all documents related to the trademarks, which are in the possession of the Sales Partner, particularly the applications, the correspondence following the applications with the authorities, the registration certificates, documents pertaining to searches and monitoring of collisions, the database including the data (to the extent available), and agreements with third parties, if any. The duty to surrender possession shall also apply to documents, which relate to the temporary or final refusal of protection for any international registration of one of the trademarks. The registration documents are to be surrendered in the original, while copies shall be sufficient with regard to all other documents. ”

In Section M of the Distributor Agreement, the consequences of the ending of the contract are provided for. Section M (8) and (9) state as follows:
“8. As of the end of the agreement, the Sales Partner shall no longer be entitled to use in any form the name of purus, its trademarks, and other identifications. After the end of the agreement, the Sales Partner shall refrain from any other reference to the earlier contractual relationship with purus and refrain from making any statement that is intended to give the impression that the Sales Partner is still an authorized member of the purus sales network.
9. At the end of the agreement, the Sales Partner shall obtain the consent of its clients for the passing on and further use of their personal data, where such necessary in accordance with the laws of Canada. Where a corresponding consent exists on the part of the client, the Sales Partner is to provide purus with a complete list of the addresses of the clients, whose personal data is only to be used in line with the approval granted. All of the documents provided to the Sales Partner by purus (in particular, technical instructions, diagrams, plans, etc.) and purus advertising materials (brochures, advertising materials) are to be returned to purus when the agreement ends. "

In case of the intentional infringement of contractual obligations under item 8 and item 9 of this contractual provision, Section M (10) Distributor Agreement provides for the payment of flat rate compensation for damages totaling EUR 10,000.00 to the Claimant. The corresponding provision states:
“10. For each case of intentional breach of the provision contained in items 8 and 9 of this contractual provision, the Sales Partner undertakes to pay flat rate compensation for damages totaling EUR 10,000,00 to purus. By agreeing to pay this flat rate compensation for damages, the Sales Partner acknowledges that the aforementioned amount is not to be considered as liquidated damages. The flat rate compensation for damages is to be deducted from any other claims for compensation for damages made by purus. Any other rights and claims of purus in connection with such an infringement shall remain unaffected. ”

The Distributor Agreement provides for a fixed term until December 31, 2009 in Section L (1). After December 31, 2009, the Distributor Agreement will automatically be extended in accordance with Section L (1) sentence 2 by a further year unless it is terminated effective at the end of the term. Section L (2) Distributor Agreement provides for further automatic extension of one further year each unless the contract is terminated in writing at six months’ notice effective at the end of a month.

In addition, Section L (9) of the Distributor Agreement provides for the automatic ending of the Distributor Agreement in the case of the occurrence of circumstances that result in the basis for business ceasing to exist. Section L (9) Distributor Agreement states as follows in this respect:
“9. In the case of the occurrence of circumstances that result in the basis for business ceasing to exist, all of the obligations of the parties hereto shall be void and the agreement shall automatically end on the day of such event without notice.”

Section (3) Distributor Agreement contains the following provision:
“3. Should provisions of this agreement be or become ineffective or unenforceable or should this agreement contain gaps, the effectiveness of the remaining provisions hereof shall remain unaffected.”

In addition, Section N (5) Distributor Agreement contains the following obligation to perform mediation proceedings in case of differences of opinion during the performance and ending of the Distributor Agreement:
“5. Should differences of opinion arise between the parties during the performance or ending of this agreement, the parties hereto undertake initially to enter into mediation proceedings on the basis of the rules of procedure of the mediation center of the Nuremburg Chamber of Commerce and Industry for Mid-Franconia.

Section N (9) Distributor Agreement contains a choice of law by the parties in favor of the substantive laws of the Federal Republic of Germany:
“9. This agreement and all purchase contracts and deliveries of goods performed under it between purus and the Sales Partner shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the substantive laws of the Federal Republic of Germany. The Vienna UN Convention on the International Sale of Goods dated April 11, 1980 (“CISG”), the Hague Convention relating to a Uniform Law on the International Sale of Goods and the Hague Convention relating to a Uniform Law on the Formation of Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, both dated July 1, 1964 shall not apply. ”
After the conclusion of the agreement, the Claimant began to deliver goods to the Respondent under the names ECORASTER and ECOGRID for sale in the U.S.A.

Within six months from the signing of the Distributor Agreement, the Claimant supplied contractual products to the Respondent under the name ECORASTER, and the Respondent began performing sales of the contractual products before the end of April 2008. In 2008, a total of nine deliveries were made. The Respondent ordered contractual products from the Claimant on April 22, 2008, May 29, 2008, August 15, 2008, August 21, 2008, September 02, 2008, September 09, 2008 September 15, 2008, September 17, 2008, and on November 19, 2008 (cf. Exhibit Bundle SK18-1 to SK18-11).

The Respondent advertised among other places on the internet, marketed, and sold exclusively contractual products of the Claimant during the term of the Distributor Agreement under the names HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, or HOMEGRID. Although the Respondent always and without exception sold the ECORASTER products of the Claimant under these names, the Respondent did not use the names ECORASTER and ECOGRID for these products.

The parties never spoke about the application for the trademarks either within the first six months after the conclusion of the agreement nor later during the term of the Distributor Agreement. There were also no discussions between the parties on the obligation of the Respondent under Section H (7).

The Respondent did not register the names HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOMEGRID in either the U.S.A. or in Canada during the term of the Distributor Agreement either as word or image marks. During this time, the Respondent made no attempt to register the trademarks either, and it also failed to inform the Claimant that it had failed to register the marks. The Respondent also never informed the Claimant of any legal or factual obstacles to the registration of the marks in the U.S.A. and in Canada from its perspective.

At no time during the contractual relationship did the Respondent submit any proposed designs to the Claimant for designing image marks relating to HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOMEGRID. The Claimant, however, also did not request this.
After the conclusion of the Distributor Agreement, the parties only communicated within "the usual course of trade,” i.e., about orders, deliveries, and invoices.

On July 01, 2008, the Claimant applied for the registration of the mark ECORASTER with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (“USPTO”) as a word mark (Standard Character Mark). The registration of this mark took place on September 08, 2009 (Exhibit SB3). On July 23, 2008, the Claimant submitted a corresponding application for registration of the ECORASTER trademark to the Canadian Patent and Trademark Office (“CIPO”). The registration of this trademark took place on August 29, 2011.

In addition, the Claimant established Purus North America Inc. in 2011. For this purpose, the Claimant began negotiations in 2010 with the Respondent with the intention of transferring the Distributor Agreement to Purus North America Inc. In this connection, the Respondent wished to renegotiate the Distributor Agreement and made a request for the non-compete clause in Section D (2) of the Distributor Agreement and the provisions in Section H (7) and (8) of the Distributor Agreement to be deleted. In the end, both the intended transfer of the Distributor Agreement to Purus North America Inc. and the adjustments that the Respondent wanted to make to the Distributor Agreement failed.
The Claimant terminated the Distributor Agreement by letter dated June 22, 2011 (Exhibit SB2) and therefore ended the contractual relationship as of December 31, 2011.

title.bd: Events after the Ending of the Contractual Relationship

item.p: On January 01, 2012, the Respondent registered the names HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID as U.S. trademarks (Exhibits SK4, SB13 and SB14). On December 11, 2012, the USPTO registered the trademark STABILIGRID under registration number 4,259,085 (Exhibit SK5) and on January 01, 2013, it registered the trademark HOOFGRID under registration number 4,269,608 (Exhibit SK6). For both trademark registrations, the Respondent gave an explanation of its intent to use. The Respondent produces its own products and sells them under the trademarks HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID. In April 2012, after the sale of the first newly manufactured HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID products, the Respondent submitted an explanation on the use of the trademarks.

In an application dated January 11, 2012, the Respondent registered the names HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID with CIPO as word marks. Its USPTO registrations formed the basis of these CIPO applications. According to research by the arbitral tribunal, the registration of the marks HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID in the Canadian register took place under reg. nos. TMA842215 (STABILIGRID) and TMA842216 (HOOFGRID) on February 05, 2013.

On January 16, 2012, as a result of the ending of the Distributor Agreement, the Claimant commissioned its German legal representative to request the HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOMEGRID trademarks from the Respondent.

On January 20, 2012, the Claimant learned that the Respondent had registered the trademarks HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID with the USPTO only with effect as of January 1, 2012 on its own behalf. This was determined in a trademark search performed by the Claimant’s legal representative on January 19, 2012.

In a letter dated January 30, 2012, Claimant made a request to the Respondent to transfer the aforementioned trademarks to it (Exhibit SK8). The Respondent rejected this request in a letter dated February 01, 2012 (Exhibit SK9).

Another search was performed on February 09, 2012, in which the Claimant’s legal representative determined that the Respondent had then also registered the trademarks HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID in Canada. The claimant’s legal representative informed the Claimant thereof by letter dated February 10, 2012 (Exhibit SK17).

On April 22, 2013, the Claimant applied to register the trademark HOMEGRID with the USPTO. The Claimant did not submit a sample when making the application. This trademark has not been registered to date.

In accordance with the undisputed submission by the Claimant, the Respondent ordered approximately 40,000 m2 of ECORASTER products annually during the term of the Distributor Agreement. Taking into account its delivery price of EUR 10.00/m2, the Claimant lost revenues of at least EUR 400,000,00 annually.

The Respondent is selling its products at a price significantly in excess of EUR 10.00/m2. According to the submission by the Claimant, the Respondent is selling the smaller version of its product at a price of at least EUR 21.90/m2 and the larger version for at least EUR 27.00/m2. This submission was not disputed and is therefore to be considered conceded.
The Respondent’s margin is 10% of the sale price. The Claimant’s corresponding margin for ECORASTER products is 5%-10 %.

On May 21, 2014, the Respondent advertised its products under the names HOOFGRID and STABILIGIRD [sic] on its website www.ecoterr.com. In addition, the Respondent advertises its products with photos that were either created by the Claimant or that show the Claimant’s contractual product ECORASTER, but not the Respondent’s product.

In a written pleading to Nuremburg Chamber of Commerce and Industry for MidFranconia dated May 21, 2012, the Claimant applied for the holding of mediation proceedings. The Respondent stated that it would not appear for the scheduled hearing. The mediator then stated in a letter dated September 27, 2012 that the mediation had failed and had been ended. The Claimant incurred cost of EUR 497.46 for the mediation proceedings.

The Claimant claims first of all that it has a claim to the transfer of the trademarks or granting of the rights associated with the trademark applications under Section H (7) and (8) of the Distributor Agreement in conjunction with the principles of positive breach of contract, as well as Section 17 German Trademark Act in analogy. The failure to register the trademarks within the 6-month period provided for in the agreement is alleged to represent a gross breach of obligation as defined under Section 280(1) sentence 1 German Civil Code. The service owed under the agreement had become objectively impossible as a result of circumstances for which the Respondent is responsible. As a result of the passing of time, it is claimed that it is not possible for the service owed under the agreement to be performed now, but rather, the trademarks that were registered later, HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID, could only be transferred. It is claimed that for this reason the Claimant is entitled to compensation for damages incurred in addition to the original claim to performance. As a result of its failure to perform the original service obligation, the Respondent allegedly owes the transfer of the trademarks HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID registered in the U.S.A., as well as the transfer of the Canadian (applications for) word marks HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID, as well as compensation for damages as a result of the fact that the term HOMEGRID was not registered as a mark.

In particular, the Respondent knowingly failed to register the trademarks HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID with the intention of using the trademarks for the marketing of its (own) competing products, after it had built up a sales network at the expense of the Claimant. It is alleged that right from the start the Respondent had intended to use the marks for itself.

The Claimant submits that during contract negotiations, the Respondent expressed a wish to be able to sell the Claimant’s products that had been distributed up until then under the name ECORASTER or ECOGRID for the equestrian/ungulate market under the name HOOFGRID and in the construction market under the name STABILIGRID. From the beginning, the Claimant only agreed to this on the condition that when the cooperation came to an end, these products of the Claimant sold under the names HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID would only be able to be sold under these names in the future, too. This would mean that the trademarks would have to revert or be transferred back to the Claimant. The Claimant claims that it always stated that in case of the ending of the Distributor Agreement, it wished to have available to it all rights to the names HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOMEGRID. A significant concern of the Claimant was allegedly that the names HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID were always only used for the Claimant’s products and in particular not for competing products. This agreement was also made, according to its undisputed submission, in the Distributor Agreement under Section H (6 – 8),

The Claimant also submits that contrary to the claim of the Respondent the registration of the trademarks HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOMEGRID was not impossible at the time when the agreement was concluded or before it ended. Rather, the Respondent could have applied for the registration of the trademarks in the U.S.A. and in Canada within the 6-month period provided for in the agreement without any legal or factual obstacles. In the U.S.A., it is possible to support the application of trademarks on four foundations, including (1) use or (2) the intention in good faith to use the mark in commercial trade (bona fide intention to use). A corresponding declaration could have been submitted here at any time. Then, a 6month period initially begins, which may be extended to three years from the day of the approval of the application. Within this period, the proof of actual use must be submitted. In Canada, an application may be made for a “proposed trademark.” In this case, a declaration on the beginning of use in Canada must be submitted within three years. The Respondent would have been able to provide proof of use in the U.S.A. and Canada within the prescribed period of 3 years because the Respondent itself admits that it distributed products under the aforementioned trademarks in the U.S.A. and Canada. The affixing of the trademark directly onto the product is not necessary for this. It would be sufficient, for example, to submit advertising material to prove that the trademark was used in the U.S.A. or in Canada (for all of the classes at issue).

For its own registration of the trademarks in the U.S.A., the Respondent submitted a declaration of intended use, for Canada, the declaration of the “proposed use” was allegedly submitted. if the Respondent was able to do so on January 1, 2012, it would have been able to apply for registration of the marks even during the term of the agreement. In this respect, no legal or factual obstacles would have existed. In the view of the Claimant, therefore, no reasons occurred that would have meant that the basis of the business would cease to exist as defined in Section L (9).

In addition, the Respondent would have been obligated to warn the Claimant of the circumstances claimed by it. The application for the HOMEGRID trademark in the U.S.A, by the Claimant on April 22, 2013 proved, however, that the application was possible for the Claimant.

The Claimant also disputes the further claim of the Respondent that the Claimant also did not meet the requirement of Section H of the Distributor Agreement because it could not approve the design of the trademark. The Claimant is of the opinion that the application for the trademarks would not have been impossible as a result of the lack of an approval of the design.

Initially, in the opinion of the Claimant, the Respondent would not have been obligated to register figurative marks. In the negotiations prior to the conclusion of the Distributor Agreement, the Claimant always emphasized that word marks should be registered. In the view of the Claimant, figurative marks could only have been registered in addition. As a result, the Respondent would only have to have had the design of the trademarks approved in advance by the Claimant if it had applied for the registration of figurative marks as an addition. Insofar as images or products of the Claimant were to be used, a licensing agreement would have been necessary in any case. It was claimed that the Respondent, however, only wanted to register word marks.

The Respondent was also allegedly obligated to do everything necessary in order to achieve the registration of the marks without any undue delay. For this reason, it should have prepared a proposal for the Claimant for the design of the figurative marks. At least it could have registered the word marks, for which no designs would be necessary in order to achieve effective protection as a mark. As a result, the Respondent at no time prepared a proposal for the design of figurative marks, so the Claimant was not able to approve anything, either. The Claimant rather relied on the Respondent acting in accordance with the agreement. The Claimant had no grounds for the assumption that the Respondent would not comply with its contractual obligation to register the trademark.

In addition, the Respondent cannot refer to opposing trademark rights held by “Hanover Architectural Products, Inc” (“HAP”). The Claimant claims that it had reached an agreement with HAP, which owns the older trademark rights to ECOGRID for the U.S.A.. This is, however, not relevant here because the Claimant also supplied its goods to the Respondent for distribution in the U.S.A. under the name ECORASTER, and the Claimant’s products were never distributed under the name ECOGRID. The Claimant was free to supply and distribute products under the name ECOGRID outside of the U.S.A., in particular in Canada, at any time.

In addition, the Claimant submits that it would be able to initiate proceedings and request an injunction against the use of the marks by the Respondent in accordance with Section 14 German Trademark Act. The Respondent has allegedly been using the names HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID since January 1, 2012 for sale of its own product, which looks confusingly similar to the Claimant’s ECORASTER product. In accordance with the image submitted as Exhibit SB28, it is alleged that it is not possible to differentiate between the Respondent’s products and those of the Claimant. In particular, the products do not necessarily have to be seen next to each other in order to answer this question. Rather, it only needs to be examined whether the relevant consumers would assume, if offered the Respondent’s product, that it was the Claimant’s product. This is claimed to be the case as a result of the extensive similarity between the two products. The Respondent therefore imitated the Claimant’s products distributed under the name ECORASTER with the products distributed under the name STABILIGRID in an impermissible manner.

The Claimant disputes that the Respondent has used the “unique marks HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID” since 2005. This was not the case because the Respondent’s company was only formed in 2006. According to the knowledge of the Claimant, Mr. Mark Rector suggested the terms HOMEGRID, HOOFGRID, and STABILIGRID as names for the sale of the Claimant’s products. Only the Claimant’s ECORASTER products were ever distributed under these names, without exception. The terms HOMEGRID, HOOFGRID, and STABILIGRID were mentioned on Mr. Mark Rector’s website.

Currently, the advertising activities of the Respondent with the names HOMEGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOOFGRID are unfolding and are offered on the Respondent’s website under these trademarks. Therefore, there is a risk of repetition. With the termination as of December 31, 2011, it is claimed that the Respondent lost the right to distribute contractual products under these names.

With regard to the asserted flat-rate minimum damages of EUR 20,000.00 and the application for a determination, the Claimant submits that the failure to register the marks STABILIGRID and HOFGRID [sic], the refusal to hand these over to the Claimant and the use of the marks in commerce represent at least one breach of contract each by the Respondent. According to the provisions of the Distributor Agreement, all rights to the marks were to be transferred to the Claimant with effect as of the end of the Distributor Agreement. It is also claimed that therefore after the ending of the Distributor Agreement only the Claimant would be entitled to use the HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOMEGRID marks. Nevertheless, the Respondent is continuing its advertising on its website www.ecoterr.com using the names HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID. It addition, since the ending of the Distributor Agreement, the Respondent has allegedly no longer been selling the Claimant’s products under the names HOMEGRID and STABILIGRID but rather plagiarized versions. In addition, the Respondent is advertising by using images belonging to the Claimant or images including the Claimant’s products and not the plagiarized version made by the Respondent. The Claimant further claims that irrespective of the breaching of trademark rights and image rights, the conduct of the Respondent also represents an anticompetitive violation because customers would assume that they are still being supplied with the Claimant’s products – as shown on the images – rather than with the Respondent’s plagiarized versions. The Respondent’s customers would make purchases in the mistaken assumption that they were purchasing the Claimant’s ECORASTER product. The Claimant alleges that it has lost significant amounts of revenue as a result. The losses were put at a minimum of EUR 40,000.00. Lost revenue could be set at a level considerably higher than EUR 400,000.00 taking into account a successful sales strategy and the associated increase in revenue. The Claimant further asserts that the Respondent did not have to pay any development cost, with the result that it is probably able to realize significantly higher profits than the Claimant. The Claimant was therefore able to support its claim for compensation for damages both on the basis of the agreement and also on the basis of Section 14 German Trademark Act, and Sections 9, 3, 4(9), 5(1)(1) and (1)(3) German Act Against Unfair Competition.
The Respondent admitted that it was using the marks STABILIGRID and HOFGRID [sic]. It claimed that the use of the marks ECOGRID and ECORASTER was not at issue,
The circumstances under which the registrations of the trademarks took place prove the premeditation of the Respondent. It obviously registered the marks in 2011 with effect as of 01/01/2012.
The Respondent disputes the claims asserted by the Claimant. The Claimant first of all had no right for the rights to be transferred.

By using the HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID trademarks, the Respondent claims that it is simply using marks that it created in 2005 for its own sales purposes. In 2005, it is claimed that the Claimant’s agent, ProEquus AT, had negotiated with the Respondent on the HOOFGRID business already. The same applies to HOMEGRID. It was not subject of these arbitration proceedings but was also mentioned under Section H and not shown on a product, either.

The Respondent claims that it did not intentionally circumvent the Distributor Agreement either, but that after the end of the agreement, it developed its own product for which it intended to use the trademarks (cf. Exhibit SB5). Prior to receiving the notice of termination, the Respondent made no plans or execution of any product design or production.

Initially, the Claimant allegedly showed no interest in the HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID marks. If the Claimant had really wanted to implement the Distributor Agreement, it would have been able to insist on fulfillment of Section H on October 9, 2008, i.e., 6 months after the signing of the agreement and must have known that no registration of marks had been performed in accordance with Section H (7) of the Distributor Agreement. After the Respondent successfully developed its own product, the Claimant apparently regretted its decision and asserted claims with regard to the products manufactured by the Claimant. It is alleged that the real issue was that the Claimant wanted to take over the Respondent’s market share. This is contrary to Section H, which does not permit the Claimant to take new business away from the Respondent. It is also claimed that this is contrary to paragraphs L 9 and N 3 of the Distributor Agreement, which contains both German and U.S. legal principles, according to which a contractual provision is non-binding in case of prevention as a result of infeasibility and “is separable from the contract” (Section 242 German Civil Code).

The Respondent objects to the claim to a transfer of the HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID trademarks on the grounds that the provisions of Section H Distributor Agreement could not have been performed. The impossibility of the performance is a prevention of the fulfillment of the agreement. From the beginning, the Claimant knew that Section H would become invalid because the basis of the business would cease to exist, be invalid, and infeasible, and the Claimant allegedly added Section L (9) (the basis of the business ceasing to exist) and Section N (3) (invalid/infeasible) itself to the Distributor Agreement.

In addition, the Respondent submits that the registration of the trademarks in the U.S.A. and in Canada would have been infeasible because there were allegedly no products using the trademarks during the term of the agreement, which could have been submitted together with the entry, which is necessary in accordance with 15 U.S.C. § 1058 (b)(1)(C). The registration of non-existent marks is not accepted in either the U.S.A. or in Canada. An “intention to use” registration would allegedly not have been possible, either. This would have been invalid after 36 months if no samples were submitted. The 6-month deadline for the Distributor Agreement expired on October 09, 2008, so that a sample would have had to be submitted not later than by October 09, 2011. Such sample was, however, not yet available as of October 09, 2011, with the result that no “intention to use” registration would have been possible and would have been ineffective and infeasible. In addition, the Respondent would not have been able to submit the necessary affidavit, in which it would have had to declare that it actually intended to use the trademarks on goods. Without a product identified with the HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID trademarks and without the honest intention to create a product of this kind, the Respondent would not have been able to sign the affidavit without committing perjury. There was, however, no intention of using the HOOFGRID or STABILIGRID trademarks on goods in the U.S.A. and in Canada.

The Respondent also claims that there is no provision according to which the Respondent would have to try to maintain the registration or submit applications without any prospect of success. It was also claimed that there was no provision in the Distributor Agreement that would obligate the Respondent to create a new product.

The Respondent further objected that the Claimant frustrated the performance of the obligations under Section H of the Distributor Agreement because it was the only one that could approve the design of the trademarks. Section H (8) required the registration of a design mark and not of a word mark. According to the Distributor Agreement, the design of figurative marks would have to be similar to the design of the ECORASTER and ECOGRID marks. It was claimed, however, that the Claimant did not hold a registration for the ECOGRID marks in the U.S.A. and in Canada. This trademarks, rather, had been registered in favor of HAP in the U.S.A. since April 15, 2003 and in favor of Terrafirm Solutions LTD. in Canada since February 09, 2006. The Claimant allegedly knew that there would not be a design available for approval within the 6-month period and therefore Section H (7) of the Distributor Agreement would not be possible. The marks registered under the name of the Respondent in Canada and in the U.S.A. were not figurative marks, but rather simple word marks. The Respondent also submits that it could not know how a design should be arranged. It would also be impossible for it to coordinate the design with the sample because there never was a sample and there was also no intention of creating a sample. The Respondent also claims that it did not directly take over the design of ECORASTER or ECOGRID for the marketing of its services with the HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, or HOMEGRID trademarks.

The Distributor Agreement had also failed to apply as a result of the fact that HAP’s lawyer required both parties to cease using the ECOGRID mark in August 2010 and the ceasing of the manufacture of products with this mark (Exhibit SB6). From August 2010 on, the Respondent was no longer able to use the ECOGRID mark and the Claimant also had to give up its use of the ECOGRID mark after finding out about the infringement of rights.

The Respondent also submits that as of the day after the ending of the agreement it was free to resume the work that it had begun in 2005 with other marks. After the ending of the Distributor Agreement, the Respondent manufactured its own product, which was supposed to bear the marks. The product manufactured by the Respondent would have been used as a sample for the registration of its trademarks in the U.S.A. and Canada.

This was also confirmed by the fact that the Claimant never submitted a formal complaint to the trademark authorities in the United States or Canada. It allegedly knew that it did not have any right to the trademarks.

The Respondent claims that it was never aware that the registration of the marks would not have been possible within 6 months. It is not an expert in the area of trademark registrations and Section H of the Distributor Agreement also did not require corresponding knowledge of U.S. and Canadian trademark laws.

The Claimant, on the contrary, allegedly had formidable knowledge of U.S. trademark law because it submitted an application in July 2008. The Respondent, on the other hand, claims to have no experience with this. The Claimant allegedly could also not accuse the Respondent of inactivity because the Distributor Agreement did not provide for such an activity. Rather, the Claimant was aware that there were no products identified with the names HOOFGRID or STABILIGRID. With regard to Section H (7) Distributor Agreement, the Respondent further states in its reply (p. 4): “The provision also failed to apply and therefore lapsed. In the knowledge that no application had been submitted, the Claimant made the decision to terminate the agreement.” Subsequently, the Respondent claims that it went on to build its business back up.

Section H (8) of the Distributor Agreement allegedly also failed to apply because it presumed that marks would have been registered and therefore could also be transferred. In the U.S.A., the lack of action and fault of the Claimant are to be taken into account in the determination of a breach of contract.

The Respondent further submits that it is not responsible for a breach of contract that would be grounds for a claim to injunctive relief on the part of the Claimant. This is because the Claimant did not make any submission that the Respondent was using the trademarks ECORASTER or ECOGRID. Rather, the Respondent claims, it has used the “unique” trademarks HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID since 2005. By using the trademarks HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID, the Respondent was going back to the trade names that it used in 2005 within its production activities. The Respondent claims to have used the trademarks HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID in 2005 as a marketing tool. For this purpose, the Respondent purchased corresponding domain names for HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID initially in 2005 and purchased further names in the subsequent years. It claims that it marketed its service for the sale and installation of soil support systems as early as 2005 under the trade names HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID. The Respondent claims that it should have been able to use its trademarks at will. It registered the HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID trademarks immediately after the ending of the Distributor Agreement because these marks were allegedly always the exclusive marks of the Respondent. It is asserted that the Claimant had no claim to the Respondent’s trademarks; the provisions of the Distributor Agreement would not be revived.

In addition, the Respondent disputes that there is no way of differentiating its HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID products from the Claimant’s ECORASTER products. Not only the appearance and dimension of the two products are different, but the Respondent’s products are labeled with the HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID trademarks. The Respondent also sells a product that is “made in U.S.A.,” while the Claimant sells a product not made in the U.S.A.. There is therefore no risk of any confusion between the two products on the part of consumers.

The Respondent submits in connection with the claim for compensation for damages that has been submitted that the Claimant did not make a submission that the Respondent was using the Claimant’s ECOGRID and ECORASTER trademarks. Instead, the Respondent was using its own HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID trademarks for the marketing of its products. The Claimant also made no submission on the fact that the Respondent was responsible for intentional actions. The Respondent allegedly also at no point breached obligations to act or to refrain from acting. With regard to the images used on its website, the Respondent refers to the fact that the Claimant never made any objection to the use of images and that the communication between the Respondent and the representative of the Claimant, Mr. Adam Isbitsky, with regard to the online content and images started in 2012 with the aim of preventing any confusion within the market, and both parties made open efforts to discuss all issues. Finally, the images had nothing to do with the current trademark dispute or Section H (8) of the Distributor Agreement and the Claimant allegedly suffered no damage.

The Claimant most recently submits the following motions (cf. complaint by the Claimant dated May 08, 2013 after adjustment of the motions by the written pleading dated April 28, 2014):
I.
The Respondent is ordered
1.
to transfer the trademarks “STABILIGRID,” reg. no. 4,259,085 and “HOOFGRID,” reg. no. 4,269,608, in the Register of the United States Patent and Trademark Office to the Claimant and for this purpose to give its consent to the United States Patent and Trademark Office to transfer the trademarks to the Claimant and to submit the required declarations, and
2.
to transfer the trademarks “STABILIGRID,” application no. 1559381, and “HOOFGRID,” application no. 1559376, registered with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office, to the Claimant and to give its consent to the Canadian Intellectual Property Office to record the transfer of rights in the registration files and to submit all of the declarations required for such purpose.
3.
Alternatively, if the applications have now become registrations, the Respondent is ordered to transfer the trademarks “STABILIGRID,” registration no. 1559381, and “HOOFGRID,” registration no. 1559376, to the Claimant and to give its consent to the Canadian Intellectual Property Office for the transfer of the trademarks to the Claimant and to submit the appropriate declarations.

The Respondent is ordered to refrain from using the trademarks “STABILIGRID” and/or “HOOFGRID” without the Claimant’s consent in business dealings in North America in connection with soil stabilization systems, particularly with the soil stabilization system “ECOGRID”, in particular from affixing the aforementioned trademarks to the above designated products or their presentation or packaging, from offering the above designated products under the above designated marks, from placing them on the market or possessing, importing, or exporting them for the aforementioned purposes and lastly from using the aforementioned marks in business documentation or in advertising.

The Respondent moves as follows (cf. written pleading dated May 08, 2014 and written pleading by the Respondent dated May 27, 2014):
The Respondent only issued the motion for the motions made by the Claimant in procedural decree No. 8 Section B item II to be rejected.
Please reject all accusations made by the Claimant and decide that the Respondent is the winning party and grant the Respondent compensation for all expenses and legal fees.

In procedural decree no. 8 dated April 11, 2014, the arbitral tribunal issued notifications to the parties and decreed that the parties could provide statements by May 23, 2014 in compliance with the sequence of the questions directed at the relevant party in items 1. – 19. of said procedural decree.
