With respect to the factual submissions of the parties, reference is also made to all written pleadings by the parties.

The arbitral tribunal is competent to reach a decision on the claims asserted. The arbitration agreement provided for in Section N (6) Distributor Agreement is effective and includes all of the claims asserted by the Claimant as a result of broad interpretation. Section N (5) Distributor Agreement refers to the mediation proceedings as a “preliminary stage” in arbitration proceedings. This refers explicitly to differences of opinion in the performance and ending of the Distributor Agreement. These differences of opinion are to be clarified by arbitration proceedings if mediation is unsuccessful.

According to the wording, the choice of law in Section N (9) Distributor Agreement covers the Distributor Agreement and thus all breaches of obligation associated with it that could result in compensation for damages. In addition, the choice of law covers post-contractual claims that are provided for in the Distributor Agreement.
As can be seen in the operative parts of the judgment, the complaint is fully justified.

The Claimant is entitled against the Respondent to the claim made in item I. of the motion for the transfer and assignment of the HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID trademarks under Section H (8) of the Distributor Agreement.

In the view of the arbitral tribunal, this claim arises directly from Section H (8) Distributor Agreement. In addition, this claim would also result as a secondary claim in accordance with Sections 280(1), 249 German Civil Code.

In accordance with Section H (8) sentence 1 Distributor Agreement, the Respondent will transfer the trademarks with effect as of the date of the ending of the Distributor Agreement – i.e., from January 1, 2012 – to the Claimant. The term “trademarks” has already been defined in Section H (7) sentence 1 of the Distributor Agreement. In the opinion of the arbitral tribunal, the definition in Section H (7) sentence 1 Distributor Agreement does not clearly state whether “trademarks” refers only to the names or whether it is necessary for the names to be registered as trademarks within six months of the signing of the Distributor Agreement. The wording of the Distributor Agreement is not clear in this respect because the addition in parentheses “(the ‘trademarks’)” does not come directly after the names HOOFGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOMEGRID. The fact that Section H (8) Distributor Agreement provides for transfer of the trademarks with effect as of the date of the ending of the Distributor Agreement is against an interpretation according to which only the names are defined as trademarks, but both parties expect that a transfer of the trademarks of this kind, i.e., of just the names, has not yet occurred. The wording of Section H (8) sentence 3 Distributor Agreement is also opposed to this interpretation. It refers to “all other rights and registrations” with reference to the trademarks, i.e., specifically not the registration of the trademarks, but only of all other registrations.

Finally, however, the question of how the term “trademarks” in Section H (8) sentence 1 Distributor Agreement is to be understood can be left open because in any case, in accordance with Section H (8) Distributor Agreement, the “STABILIGRID,” reg. no. 4,259,085, and “HOOFGRID,” reg. no. 4,269,608, trademarks registered in the USPTO register and the “STABILIGRID,” reg. no. TMA842215, and “HOOFGRID,” reg. no. TMA842216, trademarks registered with the CIPO cannot be transferred to the Claimant with effect as of January 1, 2012. The specific transfer requested in the case at issue could not be performed at this time as a result of the fact that the marks had not been applied for and registered at that time.

The Respondent does have an obligation, however, to transfer the “STABILIGRID,” reg. no. 4,259,085 and “HOOFGRID,” reg. no. 4,269,608 registered in the USPTO register and marks “STABILIGRID,” reg. no. TMA842215 and “HOOFGRID,” reg. no. TMA842216 registered with the CIPO to the Claimant on the basis of Section H (8) (3) Distributor Agreement. Accordingly, all other rights and registrations in the U.S.A, and Canada with reference to the trademarks are to be transferred to the Claimant, i.e., including the concrete trademarks STABILIGRID and HOOFGRID applied for and registered only after the ending of the Distributor Agreement.

In addition to the obligation to transfer all rights and registrations, the Respondent also entered into an obligation in Section H (8) of the Distributor Agreement to grant the registration of the transfer of rights in the appropriate register and to take all necessary steps to enable or ensure the legally valid acquisition of the marks by the Claimant and the registration of the Claimant as the owner of the marks (cf. Section H (8) sentence 4 Distributor Agreement). Therefore, the Respondent will also be obligated to give consent with regard to the STABILIGRID, reg. no. 4,259,085, and HOOFGRID, reg. no. 4,269,608, trademarks registered with the USPTO to the USPTO and with regard to the STABILIGRID, reg. no. TMA842215, and HOOFGRID, reg. no. TMA842216, trademarks registered with the CIPO to the CIPO for the transfer of the trademarks to the Claimant, as well as to submit the necessary declarations.
In addition, the claim to the transfer requested in motion item I. would also arise under Sections 280(1), 249 German Civil Code).

If the debtor breaches an obligation in a debt relationship, the creditor may demand compensation for the damages resulting from this. This does not apply if the debtor is not responsible for the breach of obligation (Section 280(1) sentences 1 and 2 German Civil Code).
The debt relationship necessary in accordance with this is the Distributor Agreement that exists between the parties.
The Respondent has also breached an obligation under the debt relationship.

In accordance with Section H (7) Distributor Agreement, the Respondent was obligated to apply for the registration of the names HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID as trademarks within 6 months from the signing of the Distributor Agreement with the USPTO and the CIPO. The Respondent undisputedly did not make the application within the 6-month period. This means that a breach of obligation exists.

The Claimant incurred damage as a result of this breach of obligation with adequate causation, which is to be settled by means of natural restitution (cf. Section 249(1) German Civil Code). If the Respondent had applied for the registration of the names HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID as trademarks within the 6-month period, the marks would have been transferred to the Claimant in accordance with Section H (8) Distributor Agreement when the Distributor Agreement ended. As a result of the fact that the Respondent failed to apply for the trademark registrations, the transfer of the trademarks to the Claimant did not occur. The Respondent therefore must therefore create the same economic situation that would have existed without the damaging event by means of natural restitution (BGH NJW 85, 793) and transfer the “STABILIGRID,” reg. no. 4,259,085, and “HOOFGRID,” reg. no. 4,269,608, trademarks registered in the USPTO register to the Claimant. It must consent to and submit the declarations necessary for this transfer of the trademarks to the Claimant to the USPTO. The same applies with regard to the “STABILIGRID,” reg. no. TMA842215, and “HOOFGRID,” reg. no. TMA842216, trademarks registered with the CIPO, which must be transferred to the Claimant and consent for this submitted to the CIPO. The legal transfer must be recorded in the legal documents, and all of the declarations necessary must be submitted. As a result of the fact that the registration of the “STABILIGRID” and “HOOFGRID” trademarks in the Canadian register has already taken place, the arbitral tribunal only had to decide on the alternative application in item I. no. 2.

In accordance with Section 280(1) sentence 2 German Civil Code, this claim is not excluded because the Respondent was not responsible for its breach of obligation. The Respondent, as the debtor of the service due in accordance with Section H (7) Distributor Agreement, is obligated to provide evidence of non-responsibility (cf. Palandt/Grüneberg, BGB [German Civil Code], 73rd edition Section 280 para. 34). It did not provide corresponding evidence.

Insofar as the Respondent argues that the registration of the trademarks in the U.S.A. and in Canada would have been infeasible because during the term of the Distributor Agreement there were no products identified with the trademarks that could have been submitted as a sample with the registration, this objection does not apply.

Even the external circumstances are opposed to this. The Respondent applied for the registration of the STABILIGRID and HOOFGRID trademarks on January 01, 2012 in the U.S.A. and then in Canada on January 11, 2012 using the U.S. application and initiated the application one day after the end of the Distributor Agreement on December 31, 2012. If it was possible to apply for the registration on January 01, 2012 – and the wording of Section H (7) of the Distributor Agreement does not request any more than the application for the registration – experience shows that this would also have been possible previously.

The presence of a breach of obligation is also underpinned by the statement by the Respondent in the written pleading dated May 27, 2014, page 5, stating that it was free to begin its work with the trademark again “on the day after the termination of the agreement (January 1, 2012).” The Respondent shows here that it intentionally refrained from applying to register the trademarks within the 6-month deadline and intentionally waited for the ending of the Distributor Agreement in order to be able to finally perform the applications immediately afterward. It is irrelevant in this respect whether the Respondent was free to become active on January 1, 2012 with regard to the trademarks. The breach of obligation that exists in the failure to perform the application due within the 6-month period is not subsequently canceled as a result of later developments.

The Respondent, however, did not provide proof that convinced the arbitral tribunal that it would not have been possible for it to perform the application within the 6month period as a result of the lack of the presence of products marked with the marks.

The Claimant submitted that registration of the marks was possible both in the U.S.A. and in Canada. In the U.S.A., it would have been possible to support the application for the registration of a mark on various grounds, among other things (1) the use and (2) the bona fide intention to use the mark in commercial trade, with only a declaration by the Claimant being necessary for this with regard to the bona fide intention to use a mark for the registration of the stated goods and/or services. In this case, an initial period of six months begins within which the declaration of use can be submitted. The deadline can be extended to a total of three years from the date of the approval of the application. This legal situation in the U.S.A. is not only known to the courts but is furthermore undisputed (cf. written pleading by the Respondent dated January 01, 2014, p. 5 footnote 1). With regard to Canadian trademark law, the Claimant has submitted that in Canada, too, it is possible to apply for trademark protection for a mark without that mark having been used in legal communications. The existence of a simple intention to use is claimed to be sufficient for a “proposed trademark.” Within three years from the time of the registration of the mark, the Claimant can submit a declaration on the initiation of use in Canada. This, too, has not been disputed by the Respondent with any substantiation and is therefore to be considered conceded.

It is disputed between the parties, however, what the proof of use to be provided within three years should look like. The Claimant is of the opinion that direct affixing of the trademark name onto the product is not necessary. Rather, it considers that, for example, the submission of advertising material is sufficient proof, along with proof that the material is being used in the U.S.A./Canada and in all of the classes at issue. On the other hand, the Respondent thinks that the names HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID would have to be affixed onto the product itself.

Neither the provisions of the 15 U.S. Code § 1051 submitted by the Claimant (Exhibit SK12) nor the Canadian Consolidation Trademarks Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. T13, Art. 40 (Exhibit SK 13) explicitly state that the affixing of the mark directly onto the product is necessary. Finally, this legal question does not need to be answered conclusively, however, because in accordance with Section H (7) sentence 2 Distributor Agreement, the sales partner, i.e., the Respondent must do everything necessary to achieve the registration of the marks without unreasonable delay. The Respondent, however, at no time – either during the 6-month period or during the subsequent further duration of the Agreement – approached the Claimant in order to overcome any obstacles to registration that exist and to be able to provide the proof of use necessary from its point of view. In doing so, it culpably failed to achieve the registration of the marks without unreasonable delay.

As a result of the fact that the Respondent was obligated under Section H (7) Distributor Agreement to do everything necessary in order to achieve the registration of the marks without unreasonable delay, it cannot refer to the fact that Claimant for its part would have had to provide information on any legal or factual obstacles to the registration of the marks in the U.S.A. and in Canada prior to or during the term of the agreement. As a result of the contractual main duty that it assumed, the Respondent was rather obligated itself to obtain information on any legal and factual obstacles, if necessary through its legal representative, whose name is listed in the register, and to overcome these obstacles.

The same applies with regard to the Respondent’s objection that the Claimant thwarted the fulfillment of the obligations provided for in Section H (7) Distributor Agreement because it was only able to approve the design of the marks. Here, too, the Respondent should have taken action itself first and should have prepared a proposal for the Claimant for the design of the figurative marks. Section H (7) sentence 4 Distributor Agreement states that the design of the HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID trademarks requires the prior written consent of the Claimant before an application can be made for the registration of the names as trademarks. This provision is also in favor of the involvement of the Claimant being limited to the issuing of its agreement, while it was up to the Respondent to take care of the design of the marks and their registration.

The issue is not whether the Respondent was able to use the design of the ECORASTER and ECOGRID marks as a basis. This is because it approached the Claimant at no point and informed it that there were legal obstacles to the registration. It was, however, obligated to do so.

Consequently, the Respondent did not convince the arbitral tribunal that it was not responsible for the failure to apply for the registration of the HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID trademarks as defined in Section 280(1) sentence 2 German Civil Code.
The claim to the transfer of the trademarks is therefore granted.
The Claimant is entitled to a claim to injunctive relief in accordance with Section M (8) of the Distributor Agreement.

In accordance with Section M (8) Distributor Agreement, the sales partner is no longer entitled to use the purus name and its trademarks in any form after the end of the agreement. The contractual partner must refrain from any other reference to the earlier contractual relationship with purus and from making any statement that might give the impression that the sales partner is still an authorized member of the purus sales network.

In the present case, the Claimant terminated the Distributor Agreement in timely manner in writing on June 22, 2011 (Exhibit SB2) effective at the end of 2011. No reason was needed for termination (cf. Section L (1) of the Distributor Agreement). In particular, the termination was also possible independently of fault on the part of the Respondent.

The Claimant submitted that the Respondent had been using the HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID names since January 01, 2012 for the sale of its products, advertising with the names HOMEGRID, STABILIGRID, and HOOFGRID, and offering them on its website under these trademarks. The Respondent did not dispute this.

Insofar as the Respondent is of the opinion that it has the right to use the trademarks HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID because it has been using them since 2005 and therefore used them first, this objection does not apply. By concluding the Distributor Agreement, the Respondent expressly entered into an obligation to refrain from using the trademarks and other identifiers of purus after the end of the agreement, irrespective of whether there is a risk of confusion with the Claimant’s products or whether there is a risk of repetition or not. The names HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID have not yet been registered as trademarks in favor of the Claimant, with the result that the wording of Section M (8) sentence 1 of the Distributor Agreement does not yet apply. If the Respondent, however, had behaved in accordance with the agreement and had applied for the registration of the HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID trademarks in accordance with Section H (7) Distributor Agreement within the 6-month deadline, the rights to these would automatically have been transferred to the Claimant at the end of the Distributor Agreement (cf. Section H (8) of the Distributor Agreement). As a result of the fact that the Respondent failed to perform the registration of the marks in a breach of its obligation, the Distributor Agreement was to be interpreted by means of the supplementary contract interpretation (cf. Section N (3) Distributor Agreement) to mean that Section M (8) also includes the case of the distributor breaching its obligation and failing to make the registration. Otherwise, the failure to perform the registration in a breach of obligation would result in the Respondent gaining the advantage from this of the rights to the names falling to it on a permanent basis. The premium this would involve for acting contrary to the agreement would be grossly unfair.

The Respondent is therefore obligated to refrain from using the trademarks “STABILIGRID” and/or “HOOFGRID” in North America for commercial purposes without the approval of the Claimant in connection with soil stabilization systems, in particular the “ECOGRID” soil stabilization system. In particular, it must refrain from using these trademarks on the aforementioned goods or affixing them onto the aforementioned goods or to their packaging. The Respondent must also refrain from offering for sale, marketing, or holding, importing or exporting corresponding goods for sale under the aforementioned trademarks, or using the marks in business documentation or advertising.

The Respondent has a claim against the Claimant to the granting of information initially under Sections 242, 260 German Civil Code on the origin and the sales channel for the goods described in motion II., in particular to the granting of information on
-
the names and address of the manufacturers, suppliers, and the commercial customers and sales locations for which they were intended and
-
the quantity of the manufactured, delivered, received, or ordered goods, as well as the prices that were paid for the goods at issue.

The right to information in accordance with Sections 242, 260 German Civil Code also applies as an accessory to claims resulting from breaches of obligation and infringements of obligations to cease and desist, as regulated in this case in Section M (8) Distributor Agreement. This is intended to make possible the identification of claims for compensation for damages in case of breaches of the obligation to cease and desist in accordance with Section M (8) Distributor Agreement.

Sections 242, 260 German Civil Code are the basis for an obligation to provide information if the legal relationship existing between the parties results in the entitled party is uncertain in a justifiable manner of the existence of scope of its right and the obligated party can easily provide the necessary information to rectify the uncertainty (constant case law since RGZ judgment II 310/22, May 4, 1923, 108, 1, 7 – Happy Face, see also Ann/Hauck/Maute, Auskunftsanspruch und Geheimnisschutz im Verletzungsprozess [Right to Information and Protection of Secrecy in Infringement Litigation], Cologne 2011, pp. 32 et seqq.). This prerequisite is met here because only the Respondent knows the sales channels for the goods identified with the HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID trademarks and therefore only it can provide information on this.
Otherwise, the claim to information that was asserted also arises under Sections 17, 19 German Trademark Act. In the opinion of the arbitral tribunal, this regulation applies to the case at issue.

title.bd: Flat-Rate Claim to Compensation for Damages

item.p: The Claimant can require compensation for damages from the Respondent under Section M (10) Distributor Agreement totaling EUR 20,000.00.

The claim exists because the Respondent intentionally breached its obligations under Section M (8) sentence 1 of the Distributor Agreement by using the HOOFGRID and STABILIGRID trademarks each after the ending of the agreement and applied for the registration of these trademarks. The Claimant gave concrete details of this in its written pleading dated February 10, 2015, stating that the registration of HOOFGRID as a trademark and its use, as well as the registration of STABILIGRID as a trademark and its use, both represent an infringement.

Therefore, under Section M. (10) Distributor Agreement, flat-rate compensation for damages of EUR 10,000,00 is payable for each infringement, i.e., a total of EUR 20,000.00. The Respondent must pay this sum to the Claimant.
The declaration requested in motion item V. is also justified.

The application for a declaration is permissible. The Claimant may not have demonstrated that it has an interest worthy of protection in an immediate declaration and that therefore there is an interest in a declaration (Section 256 German Code of Civil Procedure), but there does not need to be an interest in declaration of this kind for an arbitral tribunal because consideration of the limited resources of the public justice authorities is not necessary with regard to a private arbitral tribunal. An economic interest in the declaration is therefore sufficient (cf. Musielak-Voit, ZPO [German Code of Civil Procedure], Section 1046 Code of Civil Procedure para. 2). The economic interest of the Claimant results in the present case from the compensation for damages that may be received as a result of the desired declaration.

In this case, the Claimant wishes the declaration of the obligation of the Respondent to pay compensation for damages made on the basis of the legal relationship that exists between it and the Respondent based on the Distributor Agreement. Although this legal relationship ended when the agreement ended on December 31, 2011, there may still be legal consequences from it for the present and for the future. The legal relationship that exists between the parties can therefore definitely still be grounds for a declaratory action.

In detail, the Respondent requests a declaration that Respondent is obligated to reimburse the Claimant for all damage incurred and that the Claimant will incur in the future in connection with the failure to apply for the registration of the STABILIGRID, HOOFGRID, and HOMEGRID trademarks in the U.S.A. and in Canada in accordance with Section H (7) Distributor Agreement dated April 09, 2008, the failure to transfer the trademarks in accordance with item I, the unlawful use of the STABILIGRID and/or HOOFGRID trademarks, and, in particular, the actions described in motion II, taking into account the flat-rate minimum damages in accordance with item IV.

Any resulting claims for compensation for damages result from Section 280 German Civil Code. The failure to register the trademarks STABILIGRID, HOOFGRID, and HOMEGRID represents a breach of the obligations of the Respondent under Section H (7) Distributor Agreement, from which further damage could arise in connection with the failure to transfer the trademarks. Reference is made to statements hereinabove that apply accordingly to the name HOMEGRID. Use of the STABILIGRID and/or HOOFGRID trademarks contrary to the agreement, in particular in breach of Section M (8) Distributor Agreement, also represents a breach of obligation and on these grounds is justification for compensation for damages under Section 280(1) sentence 1 German Civil Code. The Respondent also did not prove that it was not responsible for the corresponding breaches of obligation. The incurring of damage is also probable with regard to the failure to register the trademarks because the Respondent has now applied for the registration of the trademarks for itself. With regard to use contrary to the agreement, the incurring of damage is also probable because any use by the Respondent contrary to the agreement results in an obligation to pay flat-rate compensation for damages in accordance with Section M (10) Distributor Agreement.

As a consequence, the Respondent is therefore obligated to reimburse the Claimant for all damage it has incurred and will incur in the future in connection with the failure to apply for registration of the STABILIGRID, HOOFGRID, and HOMEGRID trademarks in the U.S.A. and in Canada in accordance with Section H (7) of the Distributor Agreement dated April 09, 2008, the transfer of the marks in accordance with motion I of the statement of claim, the unlawful use of the STABILIGRID and/or HOOFGRID trademarks and, in particular, the actions described under item II, taking into account the flat-rate minimum damage in accordance with item IV.

The cost decision is based on Section 35.2 of the DIS Arbitration Rules. According to these provisions, the losing party must bear the cost of the arbitration proceedings. Therefore, as the losing party, the Respondent is responsible for the cost of the arbitration proceedings including the cost incurred by the Claimant necessary for appropriate legal prosecution.

The arbitral tribunal is simply making a decision of the grounds for cost in this arbitration award. The arbitral tribunal will issue a separate Cost Arbitration Award with a decision on the amount of cost, which the Respondent will be obligated to pay.

title.bd: Determination of the Value in Dispute

item.p: The arbitral tribunal has set the value in dispute at EUR 816,497.46 (cf. Section 40(2) DIS Arbitration Rules). This amount is made up of: a partial amount for the motion in item I. of EUR 400,000.00, a partial amount for the motion in item II. of EUR 250,000.00, a partial amount for the motion in item III. of EUR 50,000.00, a partial amount for the motion in item IV. of EUR 20,000.00, a partial amount for the motion in item V. of EUR 96,000.00 and a partial amount for the motion in item VI. of EUR 497.46.

The arbitral tribunal refers firstly to the justification of the fixed value in dispute based on the statements in procedural decree no. 11 dated August 20, 2014. In addition to this and taking into account the submission of both parties regarding the amount of the value in dispute, in particular taking into account the statements made by the Claimant in its written pleadings dated September 15, 2014, February 10, 2015, and March 30, 2015, the arbitral tribunal states the following:

In the view of the arbitral tribunal, the motion in item I. is to be set at EUR 400,000.00. In the written pleadings dated February 10, 2015 and March 30, 2015, the Claimant submitted that the value in dispute should be set at EUR 100,000.00 at most. The starting point for the determination of the value in dispute is the value of the STABILIGRID and HOOFGRID trademarks. The Claimant has now performed a calculation of the value of the trademarks based on a revenue factor and claims that the calculation of the value in dispute in this case should be based on a maximum of a revenue multiple of 0.20. The arbitral tribunal agrees with the Claimant in that the application of the whole revenue, i.e., a revenue factor of 1.0 does not appear to be appropriate in this case. When determining the value, however, it must first of all be taken into account that the precise revenue of the Respondent generated through the sales of systems using the STABILIGRID and HOOFGRID trademarks is unknown. The Claimant stated in the written pleading dated May 22, 2014 that the Respondent had ordered approximately 40,000 m2 of the products during the term of the Distributor Agreement. This would generate annual revenue of EUR 400,000.00 at a sale price of EUR 10.00 per m2. The Claimant also submitted without dispute, however, that the Claimant sells the smaller version of its products for a price of at least EUR 21.90/m2 and the larger version for at least EUR 27.00/m2. The average between these two potential revenue values is EUR 978,000.00. If these potential revenue values and the statements made by the Claimant in its written pleading dated March 30, 2015 are taken into account as revenue factors when determining the value of the trademarks, the arbitral tribunal considers the setting of the value in dispute for the motion under item I. at a level of EUR 400,000.00 for both trademarks to be appropriate and proper. This would correspond to average revenue of EUR 978,000.00, with a revenue multiple of 0.4; this takes sufficient account of the Claimant’s concerns in the view of the arbitral tribunal. The arbitral tribunal is able to understand the considerations of the Claimant regarding the value of the trademarks but is also of the opinion that this is not directly comparable because in this case the issue is the transfer of the trademarks, which is not comparable with the global brands that the Claimant used as examples. The value in dispute of trademarks that could be of definite importance to companies would move toward 0 – if one follows the train of thought of the Claimant consistently –, the lower the revenue generated with them is. In the case at issue, this would not be in line with the interests involved. Therefore, the graphic submitted by the Claimant also shows a higher revenue multiple the lower the revenue becomes.

Decision BGH, GRUR 2006, 704 submitted by the Claimant as grounds for its concerns and its further statements in the written pleading dated February 10, 2015 in connection with the provisional value in dispute set by the arbitral tribunal for the preliminary injunctions are – with regard to the alleged regulated value in dispute – registration cases. This is not comparable here. Instead, the examples provided by the Claimant in its written pleading dated March 30, 2015 on complaints relating to omissions under trademark law are more applicable. Here, “a very slight economic significance” can be presumed because the parties, for example, have entered into an international agreement for the sale of the products and have taken into account registrations in the U.S.A. and in Canada. A value in dispute for each trademark of EUR 125,000.00 therefore appears appropriate. It should also be taken into account that the Claimant initially applied for a fine of up to EUR 250,000.00, which underlines the value of the matter at this scale. Therefore, the arbitral tribunal sets the value in dispute for the motion under item II. at EUR 250,000.00.

The value in dispute for the motion under item III is, contrary to the original opinion given in procedural decree no. 11 dated August 20, 2014, taking into account the submission by the Claimant in its written pleading dated September 25, 2014, to be set at EUR 50,000.00. The Respondent did not counter the amount of EUR 50,000.00 proposed by the Claimant, so this seems appropriate to the arbitral tribunal.

The motions in item IV. and item VI. as motions for benefits stating figures should be set at the value of the desired payment. As grounds for the level of the value in dispute in the motion in item V., reference is made to the statements in the procedural decree no. 11 dated August 20, 2014. In a deviation from the calculation period used there of 2.5 years from the end of the term of the Distributor Agreement, a duration of 3.5 years from the end of the Distributor Agreement has now been used to calculate the value in dispute. Potential minimum damage can be estimated based on a hypothetical annual profit of EUR 40,000.00 at the time of the issuing of the arbitration award at EUR 140,000.00. A value in dispute for the motion in item V. of EUR 96,000.00 results therefrom.

section.p: In the arbitration proceedings, the Arbitral Tribunal hereby issues the following

p.bd: The Respondent is sentenced to refund the Claimant the DIS processing fee of EUR 8,664.97 and the cost and expenses of the arbitral tribunal totaling EUR 56,571.33, as well as the cost of its own legal prosecution of EUR 45,715.72, as well as the cost incurred during mediation of EUR 497.46.

section.p: The cost arbitration award is based on the following

item.p: The arbitral tribunal sentenced the Respondent in the award dated September 8, 2015 (“Arbitration Award”) in accordance with the application and determined in the basic cost decision that the Respondent as the unsuccessful party must be responsible for the cost of the arbitration proceedings including Claimant’s cost and for appropriate prosecution. The court set the value in dispute in the arbitration award at EUR 816,497.46 (cf. Section 40(2) DIS Arbitration Rules).

The arbitral tribunal asked the Parties in proceedings decree no. 19 dated May 26, 2015 to provide each other with information about and proof of the cost on either party and then to issue an opinion on the cost breakdown of the other party.
The Claimant issued an opinion in correspondence dated June 8, 2015 and June 18, 2015 and the Respondent issued an opinion on this in correspondence dated June 8, 2015 and June 22, 2015.

After detailed examination of the aforementioned correspondence with proceedings decree no. 20 dated July 07, 2015, the arbitral tribunal requested the submission of the relevant invoices in which the stated hours had been charged, if this had not already been done. It also requested information on the extent to which the hours stated before the arbitration action was initiated on May 8, 2013 are connected with the performance of the present arbitration proceedings and to issue a legal affidavit of their accrual and connection with the arbitration action.

In addition, the parties were requested to issue a legal affidavit stating that the other hours and translation cost were incurred in connection with the present arbitration proceedings and the stated fees have been paid or are still to be charged and paid. The Claimant was also asked to provide information on the relevant number of accrued hours and the hourly rate charged with regard to the invoices of the procedural representatives submitted to date. The Claimant was also requested to provide information on the basis for the fees of LeClairRyan LLP law firm and law firm Akermann LLP in detail and to issue a legal affidavit stating that the fees stated in this respect were charged and paid or are still to be paid and that the fees stated are connected with the performance of these arbitration proceedings.
The Claimant gave an opinion on proceedings decree no. 20 in correspondence dated July 20, 2015 and the Respondent gave an opinion on this in correspondence dated July 21, 2015.
The Respondent is to reimburse the Claimant for cost as follows:

The Claimant requests from the Respondent the reimbursement of cost and expenses stated in the following (in each case excluding VAT.):
Subject matter
EUR
1
DIS processing fee
8,664.97
2
Advance payment (net) on the Arbitral Tribunal’s fee (Section 40(1), 5 DIS Arbitration Rules in connection with Annex to Section 40(5) DIS Arbitration Rules)
55,707.17
3
Arbitral tribunal expenses (net)
864.16
4
Legal fees
- Invoices Heuking Kühn Lüer Wojtek
- Invoice LeClair Ryan
- Invoice Akerman LLP
46,616.98
5

497.46

112,350.74

The Claimant explained in more detail the cost claimed in particular in its correspondence dated July 20, 2015 and in correspondence dated October 7, 2015 claimed the refunding of the other DIS processing fee requested by the DIS and paid to DIS totaling EUR 9,121.31 gross.

The Respondent gave its opinion on June 22, 2015 of the cost asserted by the Claimant and in particular made the following objections:
•
The Claimant allegedly incurred fees and cost totaling $26,596,00 (approx. EUR 23,644.38), which means that the Claimant, in comparison with the approx. $84,541.34 (EUR 75,158.94) spent almost 70% more in fees and cost than the Respondent. The Claimant’s fees and cost were alleged to be clearly inappropriate. Both parties allegedly submitted correspondence and reacted to each degree and submitted proof, nevertheless Claimant’s cost was many times higher than Respondent’s cost.
•
It was alleged that only appropriate cost is acceptable and Respondent’s cost is claimed to be less appropriate than those of the Claimant because the Respondent had to set itself the difficult task of creating all the documents in a foreign language, having been translated, and then submitting them. It was claimed that this led to misunderstandings and involved higher fees and cost.
•
The fees of the Respondent were significantly below the fees of the Claimant although the Respondent took into account eight months in 2012 and the Claimant did not assert a claim for any cost in 2012.
•
Apparently, the Claimant is claiming that it incurred cost of EUR 28,824.84 and the increase in the compensation claim by the Claimant from EUR 50,000.00 to EUR 400,000,00 and the associated increase in the advance payments by the arbitral tribunal were the cause of this. The Claimant should allegedly not be able to claim the increased cost, but rather Claimant’s cost should have been limited to the cost required in proceedings decree no. 1 totaling EUR 7,369.08.
•
In addition, it is claimed that it is unclear whether the Claimant has included cost for the application for the HOMEGRID trademark in the USA. This cost including the cost for the LeClair Ryan attorneys cannot be reimbursed because HOMEGRID allegedly does not have a product that is suitable for the trademark.
•
Claimant’s cost is allegedly excessive.
As the losing party, the Respondent is to reimburse the Claimant for cost actually incurred during the arbitration proceedings totaling EUR 110,952.02.
The cost decision is based on Section 35.2 DIS Rules of Arbitration. In accordance with this provision, the losing party must in principle bear the cost of the arbitration proceedings.
The Claimant, who won in this case, is entitled to input tax deduction. Therefore, it can only request the refunding of cost in accordance with the net amounts it spent.

title.bd: DIS processing fee and fees and expenses of the arbitral tribunal

item.p: The Respondent paid the DIS processing fee of EUR 1,000.00 net to DIS at the beginning of the arbitration proceedings. Furthermore, the Claimant paid the DIS processing fee of EUR 7,664.97 to DIS, which was additionally requested in the correspondence and cost note from DIS dated September 11, 2015 (cf. DIS payment confirmation dated September 24, 2015).

In addition, at the beginning of the arbitration proceedings, the Claimant paid the initially requested total advance payments for the arbitrator’s fees and expenses totaling EUR 12,385.00 net (provisional value in dispute: EUR 50,000.00). This includes an advance payment for expenses of EUR 1,000,00 net. In addition, the Claimant allegedly paid the further total advance payments for the arbitrator’s fees totaling EUR 49,773.77 net required in accordance with proceedings decree no. 13 dated January 8, 2015 (provisional value in dispute: EUR 934,497.46).

The DIS processing fee, the advance payments paid for the arbitrators’ fees, and the advance payments for expenses paid by the Claimant are to be calculated as follows on the basis of the value in dispute set at EUR 816,497.46 (in each case excluding VAT):

Overall, therefore, the Respondent is to reimburse the Claimant for the DIS processing fees and expenses of the arbitral tribunal, totaling EUR 65,236.30.
With regard to the cost of the Claimant’s own legal prosecution, the Respondent is to reimburse the Respondent for a sum of EUR 45,715.72.
In correspondence dated July 20, 2015, the Claimant stated that its cost for its own legal prosecution totaled EUR 46,616.98 net.

The legal representatives of the Claimant of Heuking Kühn Lüer Wojtek for the proceedings charged on an hourly basis, with a predominant hourly rate of EUR 350.00 and in some individual cases an hourly rate of EUR 275.00. The US-based law firm LeClair Ryan used by the Claimant for this purpose charged hourly rates of between $190.00 and $410.00 and the US-based law firm that was used later, Akerman, charged an hourly rate of $380.00. The Respondent was also charged on an hourly basis and paid an hourly rate for an attorney of $275.00 in this respect.

The arbitral tribunal decides at its own discretion what cost is appropriate. In doing so, the arbitral tribunal presumes that both parties will consider invoicing based on an hourly fee to be appropriate in principle. The employment of legal representatives at an hourly rate at the amounts claimed is the general rule in international proceedings with this level of complexity and scale.
Cf. Munich Higher Regional Court, SchiedsVZ 2012, 282, 286.

A corresponding obligation to reimburse cost is not unreasonable because the losing party must regularly expect to incur corresponding cost. It must therefore also be expected if there is a significant discrepancy in the level of the cost incurred by either party.

Therefore, overall, the Respondent’s argument that the cost asserted by the Claimant is excessive and was 70% higher than the cost claimed by the Respondent is irrelevant. In this respect the fact that the Claimant asserted its own legal cost of EUR 43,260.21 net and not legal cost of EUR 75,000.00, with the result that the comparison between the legal cost is between approximately EUR 23.644,38 on the Respondent’s side and EUR 43,260.21 net on the Claimant’s side. It is therefore not the case - as the Respondent states - that the Claimant spent EUR 75,000.00 on legal cost. The Claimant was charged by the legal representative for approximately 119 hours and the Respondent was charged for approximately 70 hours. The comparison of these levels of expenditure taking into account the correspondence exchanged is not a basis for calling into question the appropriateness of Claimant’s expenditure. The different hourly rates also appear to be comprehensible taking into account the regional and structural circumstances.

With regard to the legal prosecution cost claimed in detail by the Claimant. The 2.5 hours spent on the examination/registration of the “HOMEGRID” trademark and the resulting fee of EUR 901.26 is not eligible for reimbursement in this case because this expense is not directly connected with the arbitration action.

Claimant’s other legal prosecution cost totaling EUR 45,715.72 is to be reimbursed by the Respondent. In particular, in this respect the Respondent can also request compensation for measures taken to secure the “HOFGRID” and “STABILIGRID” trademarks because there is a direct factual connection between this and the arbitration proceedings. This includes in particular the translation cost claimed by the Claimant of EUR 650.00 by Lilli Translations. The cost incurred in connection with the Respondent’s authorized representative regarding a possible agreement because in this case, too, there is a direct factual connection with the present legal dispute.

The legal prosecution cost claimed by the Claimant were also necessary for appropriate legal prosecution (cf. Section 35.1 DIS Arbitration Rules). The Claimant proved this by submitting the corresponding attorney invoices in addition to breakdowns of activities (Annex bundle SK 26.1 to SK 26.21, Annex SK 27 and Annex bundle SK 28.1 and SK 28.2). The representative of the Claimant in the proceedings has also issued a legal affidavit stating that the information under Items 2.1 to 2.13 of its written submission dated July 20, 2015 is accurate and that the claimed hours were spent in connection with the performance of the arbitration proceedings, unless otherwise submitted. It also issued a legal affidavit stating that the invoices submitted with the exception of the invoice dated July 9, 2015 were paid and stated that it was assuming that the outstanding invoice would be paid soon. In addition, it assured that the activities by the US attorney Reif on the one hand through the LeClair Ryan law firm and on the other hand through the Akerman law firm were invoiced and were paid by the Claimant. Overall, by submitting the attorney’s affidavit, the Claimant satisfied the requirements for the justification of the legal prosecution cost.
Cf. OLG Munich, SchiedsVZ 2012, 156, 157.

title.bd: Cost for the Performance of the Mediation Proceedings

item.p: The Respondent is also obligated to reimburse the Claimant for the cost of holding the mediation proceedings totaling EUR 497.46.

In the present case, in accordance with Section N (5) of the distributor agreement, mediation proceedings were performed on the basis of the rules of procedure of the Nuremburg Chamber of Commerce and Industry for MidFranconia. The Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s Mediation Center’s rules of procedure, rules of procedure No. 1 08/12 (“Mediation Rules”) apply to this. In accordance with Section 10(5) sentence 1 of the Mediation Rules, each party will be responsible for the cost of the mediation proceedings themselves. In accordance with Section 10(5) sentence 2 of the Mediation Rules, Section 91(3) Code of Civil Procedure.

In accordance with Section 91(3) Code of Civil Procedure, the cost of a legal dispute as defined in Section 91(1) and (2) Code of Civil Procedure also include the fees incurred by conciliation proceedings before a recognized conciliation board set up by the State Justice Administration; this does not apply if more than one year has gone by between the end of the conciliation proceedings and the filing of the action. The mediations center of Nuremburg Chamber of Commerce and Industry for Mid-Franconia is a conciliation board recognized by the State Justice Administration. Section 91(1) sentence 1 Code of Civil Procedure orders that the losing party will be responsible for the cost of the legal dispute, in particular the cost incurred by the opponent, insofar as they were necessary for appropriate legal prosecution or defense. This is the case here.

The Claimant, as the winning party, submitted that it had to pay EUR 100.00 and other cost totaling EUR 397.46. This cost was not disputed either with regard to the grounds or the amount, the claimed fee and cost items are also provided for in principle in the schedule of cost of the IHK Mediation Center, which applies in accordance with Section 10(2), (3) of the Mediation Rules.

section.p: The Claimant therefore has a claim to reimbursement of this cost totaling EUR 497.46. The reimbursement of such cost is also not excluded because the Claimant submitted the application only one year after the ending of the mediation proceedings. The correspondence from the mediator is dated September 27, 2012, however, the later date taken into account “11/26/2012” indicates that the correspondence was actually drafted later, on about December 4, 2012, as stated in the fax identifier. This is not the issue in any case because the arbitration application was submitted on May 8, 2015 and therefore at the time of the formation on September 27, 2012 as the earlier date, it was submitted within one year after the end of the mediation proceedings. Insofar as the Respondent argued that the initiation of the mediation proceedings was superfluous because the Respondent was not resident in Germany and was not fluent in the German language and the Claimant had to bear the cost arising from the arbitrary initiation of the arbitration itself, this is irrelevant. The parties and therefore also the Respondent expressly entered into an obligation in Section N (5) of the Distributor Agreement for the performance of mediation proceedings.

DECLARATION OF FREDERICK W. REIF

I, Frederick W. Reif, do hereby declare and state as follows:
1.
I am over the age of 18 and am competent to give this Declaration. All of the statements herein are based on my personal knowledge.
2.
I am a partner with the law firm Wilson Elser Moskowitz Edelman hsihtasamp; Dicker, LLP in New York, NY and have held this position since July 31, 2017. Prior to that date, I was a partner with the law firm Akerman LLP.
3.
Petitioner, Purus Plastics GmbH, f/k/a purus Arzberg GmbH (“Purus”), retained me to assist it in enforcing two arbitral awards issued in an arbitration proceeding captioned Purus Plastics GmbH v. Eco Terr Distributing, Inc. (Deutsche Institutionen für Schiedsgerichtsbarkeit e. V., DIS-SV-Nü-1/13) (the “Arbitration”).
4.
On December 21, 2015, my then-firm provided counsel for Eco Terr Distributing, Inc. (“Eco Terr”) with a draft Trademark Assignment to facilitate the transfer to Purus of the U.S. and Canadian trademarks for STABILIGRID and HOOFGRID in accordance with the September 8, 2015 Award issued in the Arbitration. A copy of this draft Trademark Assignment is attached hereto as Exhibit A.
5.
Despite repeated requests, Eco Terr refused to sign this Trademark Assignment or take such other actions necessary to transfer to Purus the trademarks which were at issue in the Arbitration.
6.
I subsequently issued a letter to Eco Terr’s counsel, dated May 23, 2016, demanding that its client fully comply with the two Awards issued by the arbitral panel as a result of the Arbitration dated September 8, 2015 and October 14, 2015. In addition, I expressly informed Eco Terr’s counsel that “Purus demands that Eco-Terr immediately cease and desist from using these trademarks in any manner (including on its website or other advertising or marketing materials).” I also provided another copy of the Trademark Assignment and requested that Eco Terr execute this and return it immediately. A copy of my May 23, 2016 letter is attached as Exhibit B.
7.
Eco Terr has continued to refuse to execute the Trademark Assignment or to comply in any way with the two Awards issued as a result of the Arbitration. Eco Terr continues to utilize the trademarks STABILIGRID and HOOFGRID in commerce in the United States. Attached as Exhibit C is a portion of Eco Terr’s U.S. website (www.ecoterr.com) which was visited on February 5, 2018 reflecting the continued use of these trademarks.
I declare under penalty of perjury that the above statements are true and correct.

p.bd: Re: Purus Plastics GmbH v. Eco Terr Distributing, Inc. DIS-SV-Nü-1/13

section.p: Dear Ms. Christian:

I write on behalf of Purus Plastics GmbH (“Purus”) with respect to the captioned matter. As you are aware, my partner, Peter Chiabotti, has previously contacted you to request that your client, Eco-Terr Distributing, Inc. (“Eco-Terr”), execute a Trademark Assignment in accordance with the September 8, 2015 arbitration decision issued in this matter. By email dated February 17, 2016, you informed Mr. Chiabotti that Eco-Terr “has submitted a challenge to the orders entered by the panel and expects to receive a response.”

To date, Purus’s German counsel (Dr. Ulrike Helkenberg) has confirmed that she has not received any “challenges” by Eco-Terr to either of the decisions rendered by the arbitration panel (the “Panel”), In addition, by letter dated January 12, 2016, the German Institution of Arbitration (Deutsche Institution für Schiedsgerichtsbarkeit e. V.) confirmed that the Schiedsspruch and the Kostenschiedsspruch are, in fact, “the final decisions rendered in the above-mentioned arbitral proceeding. The arbitral proceedings have been terminated with the rendering of these decisions.” In fact, upon issuance of its decisions, the Panel was dissolved and an appeal is not possible (either to the Panel or to a court).

Nevertheless, to the extent that Eco-Terr made any filings with the Panel (or any other body) challenging those decisions, we request that you immediately forward to us copies of any such filings. If not, Purus demands that Eco-Terr fully and completely comply with the Panel’s Schiedsspruch (dated September 8, 2015) and its Kostenschiedsspruch (dated October 14, 2015). Additional copies of both are attached for your reference.

In accordance with the Schiedsspruch, Eco-Terr is obligated:
A.
To transfer the trademarks:
1.
“STABILIGRID” (registered with the United States Patent and Trademark Office under number 4,259,085) and “HOOFGRID” (registered with the United States Patent and Trademark Office under number 4,269,608) to Purus and to make all necessary statements, filings and applications to the United States Patent and Trademark Office to effect such transfer;
and
2.
“STABILIGRID” (registered with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office under number 1559381) and “HOOFGRID” (registered with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office under number 1559376) to Purus and to make all necessary statements, filings and applications to the Canadian Intellectual Property Office.
B.
To refrain from using without the prior permission of Purus the trademarks “STABILIGRID” and/or “HOOFGRID” in the course of business dealings in North America concerning ground reinforcement systems, in particular concerning the “ECOGRID” ground reinforcement system.
C.
To provide Purus with information regarding the origin and the distribution channels of the goods described above, including
-
the names and addresses of manufacturers, suppliers, commercial customers and points of sale for which the goods were intended, and
-
the amount of the manufactured, delivered, received or ordered goods as well as the prices paid for the respective goods.
D.
To pay Purus compensatory damages in the amount of EUR 20,000.00.
E.
To compensate Purus for all future and past damages and losses arising from Eco-Terr’s failure to register the trademarks “STABILIGRID”, “HOOFGRID” and “HOMEGRID” in the U.S.A, and Canada in accordance with the Distribution Agreement of April 9, 2008, and arising from Eco-Terr’s unlawful use of the trademarks “STABILIGRID” and “HOOFGRID.”
F.
To reimburse Purus for all fees and costs associated with this dispute. In the Kostenschiedsspruch dated October 14, 2015, the Panel specifically determined these costs to include the following:
1. DIS administrative fee:
EUR 8,664.97
2. Costs of the Panel:
EUR 56,571.33
3. Purus attorney fees:
EUR 45,715.72
4. Mediation costs:
EUR 497.46
TOTAL COSTS AWARDED:
EUR 111,449.48
To facilitate Eco-Terr’s compliance with the decision of the Panel, I enclose another copy of the Trademark Assignment we previously provided, Please have your client execute this Assignment and return it to my attention immediately.
With respect to the Panel’s directive that Eco-Terr refrain from using the “STABILIGRID” and “HOOFGRID” trademarks, we note that your client continues to improperly use these trademarks at present (including on its website: www.ecoterr.com). Purus demands that EcoTerr immediately cease and desist from using these trademarks in any manner (including on its website or other advertising or marketing materials). Purus will hold Eco-Terr fully liable for its unpermitted and unlawful use of these trademarks.
In the event that Eco-Terr fails to promptly comply with all aspects of the decisions of the Panel, Purus will be forced to commence enforcement proceeding in the United States against Eco-Terr pursuant to the New York Convention, 9 U.S.C.A. § 201 et seq. If forced to do so, Purus will seek to recover from Eco-Terr all damages permitted by law, as well as all costs and attorneys’ fees incurred as a result of Eco-Terr’s conduct.
I look forward to hearing from you as soon as possible.
Very truly yours,
Frederick W. Reif
